The plugin registers an instance of the link:{springapi}/org/springframework/cache/CacheManager.html[CacheManager] interface as the `grailsCacheManager` Spring bean, so it's easy to access using dependency injection.

The most common method you would call on the `grailsCacheManager` is `getCache(String name)` to access a link:{springapi}/org/springframework/cache/Cache.html[Cache] instance programmatically. This shouldn't be needed often however. From the `Cache` instance you can also access the underlying cache implementation using `cache.getNativeCache()`.

The cache tags cache with the `grailsCacheManager` bean, which they are given by name. A cache provider plugin replaces it by defining a bean of that name, and an application can do the same with a `GrailsCacheManager` of its own.

The cache annotations, and `GrailsCacheAdminService`, cache with the same bean. The field they are given their cache manager through is qualified with the name `grailsCacheManager`, so Spring injects the bean of that name, or the bean with that alias, whatever other cache managers the application context has: one the application defines for Spring's own caching, marked primary or with a `@Priority`, or the one the Spring Security plugin defines when `cacheUsers` is set. Where there is no bean of that name, as with `grails.cache.enabled: false`, the annotated methods run uncached. To cache with a cache manager of the application's own, name it `grailsCacheManager` or give it that alias. A class compiled against Grails 8, as in a plugin not yet compiled for Grails 9, keeps the cache manager Spring chooses by type until it is compiled again, and `grailsCacheManager` where Spring cannot choose.

A cache manager may have no cache of the name an annotation gives, as a `JCacheCacheManager` has none it was not configured with. The annotated method then runs uncached, and a warning names the class and the cache once for each cache manager.
